strengths: The paper addresses a useful problem: embedding a user-selected image region while preserving scene context. Combining prompt-conditioned SAM2 features with a VLM is a coherent approach that supports existing embedding workflows.

The reported MMEB results provide substantial positive evidence across 36 datasets: VIRTUE-2B improves over VLM2Vec-2B from 59.7 to 64.8, and VIRTUE-7B improves over VLM2Vec-7B from 65.5 to 68.6, with gains in both in-distribution and out-of-distribution averages.

SCaR is a potentially valuable resource, with approximately 958k training examples and 47k evaluation examples covering object, relation, and context discrimination. The reported independent human inspection of evaluation examples is a useful quality-control step.

The appendix includes meaningful architectural ablations, training configurations, generation prompts, and evaluations after SCaR finetuning. Table 7 suggests that VIRTUE preserves general embedding performance better than the tested baselines during adaptation.
weaknesses: SCaR's split integrity is insufficiently documented. RefCOCO+, RefCOCOg, and COCO-Stuff share COCO imagery, and VisualGenome also overlaps with COCO, yet the paper gives no cross-source image deduplication procedure or train–evaluation overlap audit. Independent source splits do not establish a disjoint combined benchmark. This is an important unresolved risk for the finetuned SCaR results.

The comparisons do not adequately isolate the proposed mechanism. MMEB baseline scores are imported from prior papers, without establishing matched resolution and compute; Table 6 itself shows that resolution changes VIRTUE's MMEB score by 4.7 points. The cropped-stream and Prompter ablations are useful, but a matched backbone without SAM and an unconditioned SAM-feature control are needed to distinguish prompt-conditioned entity information from additional pretrained visual capacity and tokens.

The strongest SCaR comparisons use textual coordinates for competing VLMs or remove global context through cropping. Table 6 partially addresses this with a cropped-stream alternative, but does not report that alternative under the SCaR-finetuned setting that produces the headline gains. A well-trained full-image-plus-region baseline is needed. The consistently below-chance results of several off-the-shelf VLM embedders on a ten-candidate task also warrant implementation checks and analysis.

SCaR does not yet convincingly establish compositional reasoning rather than discrimination of synthetic caption artifacts. Figure 5's automated verification checks text structure and semantic differences without checking the image. Human inspection helps, but rejection rates, agreement, and residual error estimates are absent. Similar word frequencies and caption lengths do not exclude shortcuts; text-only, image-only, and shuffled-box controls would provide stronger validation.

There are material numerical inconsistencies. In Table 2, UniME's four meta-task averages imply an overall score of approximately 63.6 when weighted by dataset counts, while its IND/OOD scores imply approximately 63.7; neither supports the reported 66.6. Table 7 likewise reports an overall 19.8 for VLM2Vec-2B after adaptation despite IND/OOD scores of 19.4/19.2. These discrepancies require reconciliation before the aggregate comparisons can be trusted.

The demonstrated scope is narrower than the general visual-interaction claims. Quantitative SCaR evaluation uses bounding boxes and ten constructed captions; point and mask prompting, large-corpus retrieval, and interactive image-to-image retrieval lack systematic evaluation. Inference latency and memory overhead from the added SAM branch are also unreported. Taken together with the unresolved evaluation controls, these limitations leave the submission below the acceptance threshold despite promising results.

strengths: The task is well motivated: region-conditioned embeddings that retain scene context could support useful interactive retrieval applications. Integrating frozen SAM2 features with a VLM is technically plausible and clearly described.

The reported MMEB results provide meaningful positive evidence across 36 datasets: VIRTUE-2B improves over VLM2Vec-2B from 59.7 to 64.8, and VIRTUE-7B achieves 68.6. SCaR finetuning also produces substantial gains over the evaluated baselines.

The paper includes substantial supporting experiments, including connector, resolution, segmentation-backbone, and token-length ablations. SCaR includes a sizeable evaluation set reportedly reviewed by two independent human inspectors, and the appendix provides training configurations and generation prompts.
weaknesses: SCaR's construction leaves important shortcuts untested. Each negative changes exactly one of three caption elements, so the correct object, relation, and scene each recur in seven of the ten candidates. A candidate-only consensus baseline could therefore exploit the construction without inspecting the image. No such baseline, text-only control, or shuffled-image/box evaluation is reported. Similar caption-length distributions do not establish that the benchmark measures grounded compositional reasoning.

Dataset separation is insufficiently documented. RefCOCO+, RefCOCOg, and COCO-Stuff share underlying COCO images, and VisualGenome also overlaps COCO. The paper reports per-source splits but does not establish image-level deduplication across the combined training and evaluation sets or audit overlap with MMEB. This is an unresolved contamination risk, rather than demonstrated leakage, but it materially limits confidence in generalization claims.

The comparisons do not fully isolate the proposed mechanism. Most SCaR baselines receive textual box coordinates or lose context through cropping. Appendix E.1 usefully includes crop-feature and randomly initialized prompter alternatives, but lacks a prompt-independent SAM-feature control and equally trained, context-preserving region baselines after SCaR finetuning. Consequently, the gains cannot be cleanly attributed to prompt-conditioned segmentation rather than additional pretrained visual features and input tokens.

The contribution is primarily an integration of existing SAM2, VLM, projection, and contrastive-learning components. Its distinction from localized representation learning, including the cited CLOC, needs stronger positioning. The experiments demonstrate usefulness but provide limited evidence that this particular integration is necessary or offers a favorable efficiency tradeoff; inference latency and memory overhead are not reported.

The evidence is narrower than the broad visual-interaction claims. Quantitative SCaR evaluation uses bounding boxes and ten synthetic caption candidates; points, masks, interactive image-to-image retrieval, and correction are not systematically evaluated. There is also no large-gallery retrieval experiment, breakdown by negative type, or uncertainty estimate to substantiate the stronger reasoning and universality claims.

Numerical reporting contains a material inconsistency: UniME-7B's Table 2 meta-task scores imply an overall average of approximately 63.6 across 36 datasets, while its reported overall score is 66.6; its IND/OOD scores also do not reconcile with 66.6. Because this baseline determines the headline 7B improvement, the aggregation needs correction. More generally, the unusually poor SCaR performance of several baselines, below the 10% random-choice level, warrants diagnostic checks.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful problem: embedding a user-selected region while retaining scene context. Combining prompt-conditioned SAM2 features with a VLM is a coherent approach that also accommodates inputs without visual prompts.

The MMEB evaluation provides substantive evidence beyond the proposed benchmark: VIRTUE-2B improves over VLM2Vec-2B from 59.7 to 64.8, with gains across all four task categories and both in-distribution and out-of-distribution subsets.

SCaR is a potentially valuable resource, with approximately one million examples, structured object/relation/scene distractors, and independent human inspection of evaluation examples. After SCaR training, the reported gains over the strongest corresponding baselines are 9.5 and 7.5 percentage points for the 2B and 7B models.

The appendix contains useful architectural ablations, including cropping and a CLOC-inspired prompter, plus training configurations, dataset-generation prompts, and analysis of performance retention after SCaR finetuning.
weaknesses: SCaR split integrity is insufficiently documented. Several constituent datasets share COCO images, and VisualGenome also overlaps COCO. The paper does not describe cross-source image deduplication or establish separation between SCaR training/evaluation and MMEB data. This leaves an important uncertainty about leakage and the interpretation of generalization results.

SCaR primarily measures selection among ten synthetically constructed captions, rather than retrieval from a realistic corpus. Element-swapping can introduce linguistic shortcuts; indeed, the unchanged object, relation, and scene each recur across most candidates. Text-only and candidate-consensus controls are missing, and similar caption-length distributions do not establish the absence of artifacts.

The central comparisons do not fully isolate the value of prompt-conditioned segmentation from additional visual features and computation. Table 6 provides helpful crop and prompter ablations, but these are not extended to the main SCaR-finetuned setting. Controls using unconditioned SAM features or shuffled/removed prompts would clarify whether improvements specifically reflect accurate region conditioning.

Quantitative interactive evaluation covers bounding boxes only. Point and mask support, interactive image-to-image retrieval, and correction through visual hints are supported mainly by architectural compatibility or selected examples. These results do not yet justify the full breadth of the interaction claims.

Reported aggregate scores contain inconsistencies. For example, UniME-7B's Table 2 category means imply an overall dataset-weighted score of approximately 63.6, rather than the reported 66.6. This affects the claimed strongest baseline and improvement margin and should be reconciled with Table 8.

The architecture mainly integrates existing pretrained components through a conventional connector and contrastive objective. Its practical contribution is promising, but unresolved benchmark controls, limited causal ablations, and missing inference-cost comparisons leave the evidence slightly below the acceptance threshold.

strengths: VIRTUE addresses a useful problem: producing embeddings that respond to user-selected regions while retaining scene context. Combining prompt-conditioned SAM2 features with a VLM provides a practical implementation supporting boxes, points, and masks.

The MMEB results provide meaningful evidence beyond the proposed benchmark. VIRTUE achieves 64.8 and 68.6 overall at 2B and 7B, improving over the strongest corresponding baselines by 5.1 and 2.0 points, with gains on out-of-distribution tasks.

SCaR is a substantial resource with approximately 958k training and 47k evaluation examples. The documented generation prompts, semantic filtering, and independent human inspection of evaluation samples are valuable.

The experimental analysis is extensive, including connector alternatives, segmentation backbones, feature lengths, prompt perturbations, point prompts, training configurations, and inference costs. SCaR finetuning produces substantial gains over the evaluated baselines.
weaknesses: SCaR's construction leaves important shortcut concerns unresolved. Every negative changes exactly one component of the correct caption, making the correct caption's components disproportionately frequent across the candidate set. Synthetic alternatives also include implausible descriptions such as a sculpture's mouth eating an apple. Caption-length distributions do not establish the absence of linguistic artifacts; language-only and candidate-consensus controls are needed before attributing performance to compositional visual reasoning.

The split protocol does not establish image-level disjointness across the combined source datasets. RefCOCO+, RefCOCOg, and COCO-Stuff share COCO imagery, and VisualGenome also overlaps COCO. Without a cross-source deduplication audit and explicit split definitions, contamination between SCaR training and evaluation remains an unresolved possibility.

The comparison does not fully isolate the proposed mechanism. Main SCaR baselines receive textual coordinates or crops that remove context, while red-circle prompting is evaluated only with CLIP. The connector alternatives in Table 9 are useful, but stronger visually prompted VLM baselines and a matched additional-encoder control would better distinguish benefits from spatial conditioning, extra pretrained visual features, and added tokens.

The architectural contribution is principally an integration of existing SAM2 and VLM components using a convolutional/MLP connector and standard contrastive learning. Its significance therefore depends heavily on convincing evaluation, yet interactive retrieval is quantitatively tested only through ten-caption synthetic candidate sets. Large-gallery retrieval and interactive image-to-image applications remain unvalidated beyond selected examples.

Several claims exceed the evidence. The advertised SCaR improvement of 15.2%–20.3% describes relative gains after SCaR finetuning; without it, the 7B improvement over UniME is only 1.5 percentage points. No repeated-run uncertainty is reported, and the explanation that the segmentation branch prevents catastrophic forgetting is not isolated from optimization effects despite unusually severe baseline degradation in Table 10.

strengths: The problem is useful and well motivated: region-specific retrieval should preserve scene context while allowing users to identify an object through visual prompts. VIRTUE provides a technically plausible implementation using frozen SAM2 features, a learned connector, and a VLM embedder.

The MMEB evaluation provides concrete positive evidence across 36 tasks. VIRTUE improves the overall score from 59.7 to 64.8 at 2B and from the strongest reported 7B baseline's 66.6 to 68.6, with gains on both in-distribution and out-of-distribution subsets.

SCaR is a substantial resource, with approximately 958,000 training and 47,000 evaluation examples. Reviewing the evaluation samples with two annotators, reporting agreement, and providing generation and filtering prompts are meaningful strengths.

The experimental coverage is substantial: architecture alternatives, resolution, segmentation model size, token count, prompt perturbations, and computational costs are examined. After SCaR training, VIRTUE exceeds the strongest corresponding baselines by 9.5 and 7.5 percentage points at 2B and 7B.
weaknesses: SCaR's split integrity is insufficiently documented. RefCOCO+, RefCOCOg, and COCO-Stuff share COCO imagery, and VisualGenome also overlaps with COCO. The paper does not explain image-level deduplication across sources or overlap with MMEB training. Consequently, it is unclear whether evaluation images or closely related region annotations occur in training through another constituent dataset. This needs an explicit overlap audit before the generalization results can be trusted fully.

The strongest SCaR comparisons do not adequately isolate the advantage over simpler context-preserving alternatives. Main-table baselines receive textual coordinates or only a crop, whereas VIRTUE receives both global imagery and a dedicated region representation. Appendix E.1 includes a useful crop-stream alternative, but does not establish a strong, matched global-image-plus-target-crop baseline under SCaR finetuning. Red-circle prompting is tested only with CLIP, and the CLOC-inspired alternative is randomly initialized rather than a pretrained localized model.

SCaR demonstrates ten-candidate synthetic caption discrimination more directly than broad compositional reasoning or practical retrieval. Its generation prompt explicitly constructs distractors to challenge crop-only methods, while some examples contain conspicuously implausible alternatives. Similar caption-length distributions do not exclude linguistic shortcuts. Text-only candidate-scoring controls, human accuracy, results by swap type, and retrieval from a larger shared candidate pool would materially strengthen the benchmark's validity.

The methodological novelty is primarily the integration of existing SAM2 and VLM components through a conventional convolutional/MLP connector and InfoNCE objective. The ablations support this design's usefulness, but do not fully distinguish segmentation-specific benefits from additional pretrained visual features and tokens. Published MMEB baseline scores also leave training and resolution matching insufficiently established; resolution alone changes VIRTUE-2B's MMEB score by 4.7 points.

Several broader claims exceed the evidence. Interactive image-to-image retrieval and corrective hinting are illustrated through selected cases rather than systematic evaluations, and SCaR-finetuned performance drops from 56.9 with boxes to 45.0 with points. The forgetting advantage is measured under one shared finetuning configuration, without establishing well-tuned adaptation baselines. No repeated-run uncertainty is reported. Overall, the results are promising, but benchmark validation and stronger controlled comparisons are needed to clear the acceptance threshold.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful problem: region-conditioned embeddings that preserve scene context. Combining prompt-conditioned SAM2 features with VLM representations is a practical, coherent approach.

The reported results provide substantial positive evidence across 36 MMEB tasks and five SCaR datasets. VIRTUE-2B improves MMEB from 59.7 to 64.8, and SCaR-trained variants outperform the evaluated embedding baselines.

The appendix contains extensive architecture ablations, prompt perturbation experiments, efficiency measurements, and implementation details. Results after SCaR training also show substantially better retention of MMEB performance than the tested baselines.
SCaR provides approximately one million examples, documented generation and filtering prompts, and independent human inspection of evaluation samples.
weaknesses: SCaR has a structural shortcut that undermines its interpretation as a visual reasoning benchmark. Each candidate set contains three negatives changing each of three caption elements. Under the specified rules, every gold element appears in seven of ten candidates, potentially allowing the correct caption to be recovered through candidate consensus without inspecting the image. Candidate-only controls and less structured distractor sets are needed; this concern does not establish that VIRTUE itself exploits the shortcut.

Cross-dataset leakage is insufficiently addressed. RefCOCO+, RefCOCOg, and COCO-Stuff share COCO imagery, and VisualGenome also overlaps COCO. The paper does not document joint image-level deduplication across training and evaluation sources or overlap checks against MMEB. Consequently, the independence of the evaluation sets remains uncertain.

Several numerical summaries are inconsistent. Averaging UniME's 36 per-dataset scores in Table 12 gives approximately 63.6, rather than the reported 66.6. VLM2Vec-7B's four grounding scores average 85.1, rather than 82.2. These discrepancies affect baseline rankings and improvement claims and require a complete aggregation audit.

Comparisons do not fully isolate the benefit of segmentation-conditioned features. Most SCaR baselines receive textual coordinates or crops that discard context. Although Table 9 includes useful cropping and Prompter alternatives, clearly specified, equally trained full-image-plus-target-crop and region-feature baselines remain necessary. Published MMEB baseline scores also leave uncertainty about matched resolution and training settings.

The architectural novelty is primarily the integration of existing components. Interactive evaluation is restricted to ten-candidate caption selection; image-to-image retrieval is demonstrated qualitatively. Without stronger benchmark controls and quantitative evaluation beyond this constructed setting, the evidence falls slightly below the acceptance threshold.
